{{short description|Measure of financial risk}}

In [[finance]], the '''Treynor reward-to-volatility model''' (sometimes called the '''reward-to-volatility ratio''' or '''Treynor measure'''<ref>{{cite book|last=Brown|first=Keith C.|author2=Frank K. Reilly |title=Analysis of Investments and Management of Portfolios|publisher=Cengage Learning|edition=9th International|pages=941|chapter=25}}</ref>), named after American economist [[Jack L. Treynor]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.investopedia.com/terms/t/treynorratio.asp|title=Treynor Ratio|accessdate=20 February 2010}}</ref> is a measurement of the [[Rate of return|returns]] earned in excess of that which could have been earned on an [[investment]] that has no [[Financial risk|risk]] that can be [[Diversification (finance)|diversified]] (e.g., [[United States Treasury security#Treasury bill|Treasury bills]] or a completely diversified [[Portfolio (finance)|portfolio]]), per unit of market risk assumed.

The Treynor ratio relates [[excess return]] over the risk-free rate to the additional risk taken; however, systematic risk is used instead of total risk. The higher the Treynor ratio, the better the performance of the portfolio under analysis.

==Formula==
<math display="block">T = \frac{r_i - r_f}{\beta_i},</math>

where <math display="inline">T</math> is the Treynor ratio, <math display="inline">r_i</math> is the return of portfolio&nbsp;<math display="inline">i</math>, <math display="inline">r_f</math> is the [[risk free rate]], and <math display="inline">\beta_i</math> is the [[beta coefficient|beta]] of portfolio&nbsp;<math display="inline">i</math>.

== Example ==

Taking the equation detailed above, let us assume that the expected portfolio return is 20%, the risk free rate is 5%, and the [[Beta (finance)|beta]] of the portfolio is 1.5. Substituting these values, we get the following:
<math display="block">T = \frac{0.2 - 0.05}{1.5} = 0.1.</math>

==Limitations==
Like the [[Sharpe ratio]], the Treynor ratio (''T'') does not quantify the value added, if any, of [[active management|active portfolio management]]. It is a ranking criterion only. A ranking of portfolios based on the Treynor Ratio is only useful if the portfolios under consideration are sub-portfolios of a broader, fully diversified portfolio. If this is not the case, portfolios with identical [[systematic risk]], but different total risk, will be rated the same. But the portfolio with a higher total risk is less diversified and therefore has a higher unsystematic risk which is not priced in the market.

An alternative method of ranking portfolio management is [[Jensen's alpha]], which quantifies the added return as the excess return above the [[security market line]] in the [[capital asset pricing model]]. As these two methods both determine rankings based on systematic risk alone, they will rank portfolios identically.
